Serving as ruler of Dubai from 1990 until his death in 2006, this Emirati royal also held the UAE premiership across two separate terms and was succeeded by his brother — who is he?
Maktoum bin Rashid Al Maktoum: 2nd vice president, 1st and 3rd prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.
An FBI man who rose to deputy director after J. Edgar Hoover's death, he secretly fed two Washington Post reporters details on Watergate under the alias 'Deep Throat' — who was he?
Ascending the Ottoman throne at age six in 1648 after his father's overthrow, this sultan reigned longer than all but Suleiman the Magnificent and was nicknamed 'the Hunter' — who is he?
Mehmed IV: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1648 to 1687.

This 12th-century Japanese samurai commander, whose older half-brother founded the Kamakura shogunate as its first shogun, was raised at Kurama-dera temple under the childhood name Ushiwakamaru — who was he?
Minamoto no Yoshitsune: 12th-century Japanese samurai. Born as the ninth son of Minamoto no Yoshitomo of the Kawachi Genji clan, his childhood name was Ushiwakamaru.

This Nigerian general seized power in a 1983 coup and ruled as military head of state, then decades later returned to lead the country as its democratically elected president from 2015 to 2023 — who is he?
Ruling 43 years as the longest-reigning king of the Neo-Babylonian dynasty, this monarch was famed for his campaigns in the Levant and his grand building projects in Babylon — who was he?
Nebuchadnezzar II: King of Babylon from 605 to 562 BC.

Stretching from the Gulf of Finland to the Ural Mountains, this medieval city-state thrived as the easternmost outpost of the Hanseatic League and let its citizens' assembly elect and depose princes — what was it?

As the eldest son of the last Austro-Hungarian emperor, this man became the last crown prince of Austria-Hungary in 1916 and later the pretender to those thrones until resigning his headship of the imperial house in 2007 — who is he?
Otto von Habsburg: Heir to the Austrian throne (1912–2011)
Coined in 1978 by Bill Mollison and David Holmgren as a rebuke to industrial farming, this whole-systems design approach borrows arrangements straight from flourishing natural ecosystems. What is it?
Permaculture: Approach to agriculture and land management.
Begun when reformer Alexander Dubček became First Secretary in January 1968, this period of liberalization in Czechoslovakia ended with a Warsaw Pact invasion that August — what is it called?

Prague Spring: Liberalisation in Czechoslovakia in 1968. The Prague Spring (Czech: Pražské jaro; Slovak: Pražská jar) was a period of political liberalization and mass protest in 
the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.

Becoming India's youngest prime minister at 40 after his mother's assassination, this leader from the powerful Nehru family later lost the 1989 election and was himself assassinated in 1991 — who was he?

Rajiv Gandhi: Prime Minister of India from 1984 to 1989. Rajiv Ratna Gandhi (20 August 1944 – 21 May 1991) was an Indian politician and pilot who served as the prime minister of India from 1984 to 1989 for two terms.

Lancashire-born and West Coast-settled, this Liberal politician became New Zealand's longest-serving head of government, holding the premiership for thirteen years until his death in 1906 — who was he?
Richard Seddon: Prime minister of New Zealand from 1893 to 1906.
As a US Attorney in the 1980s he led the federal prosecution of New York City's mafia bosses before running on a 'tough on crime' platform — which future mayor and later disbarred lawyer?
Rudy Giuliani: American attorney and politician (born 1944)
A moderate conservative swing vote nominated by Ronald Reagan, this former Arizona state judge made history in 1981 as the first woman on the U.S. Supreme Court — who is it?
Sandra Day O'Connor: American lawyer, politician and judge (1930–2023)

A close confidant of Vladimir Putin, this Russian official ran the Emergency Situations ministry for two decades before serving as Defence Minister and being tasked with supervising the war in Ukraine — who is he?
This king moved Poland's capital from Kraków to Warsaw and was the first Polish monarch from a Swedish royal house — who is he?
Sigismund III Vasa: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1587–1632), King of Sweden (1592–1599)
Crowned in 1576 after marrying Queen Anna Jagiellon, this ruler defeated a rival claimant to become the third elected king of Poland — who was he?
Stephen Báthory: Ruler of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1576 to 1586.

Punished in the underworld by standing in a pool beneath a fruit tree whose branches always pulled away from his grasp, this Greek mythological figure lent his name to the English word for teasing someone with something unreachable — who was he?
Tantalus: Greek mythological figure and son of Zeus.
This Norwegian adventurer drifted 8,000 km across the Pacific on a hand-built raft in 1947 to test his theory that South Americans settled Polynesia first — who is he?
Thor Heyerdahl: Norwegian anthropologist and adventurer (1914–2002)
Once an actor who ran the film company Red Giant Movies, he served as Tamil Nadu's Deputy Chief Minister from 2024 to 2026 before becoming the state's Opposition Leader. Who is he?
Udhayanidhi Stalin: Indian politician and former actor.
The first chairman of Gazprom and Russia's second-longest-serving Prime Minister, this 1990s politician became famous for malapropisms that turned into everyday Russian idioms — who is he?

The first governor-general of Bengal, he and Robert Clive are credited with laying the foundation of British India — then in 1787 he was impeached for corruption, only to be acquitted in 1795. Who is it?
First achieved in Australasia before spreading to Europe and the Americas, this democratic right for female voters began its 'first wave' in 1893 in English-speaking countries — what right?
Women's suffrage: Legal right of women to vote.
Ruled by dictator Mobutu Sese Seko from 1965 to 1997, this Central African nation was, by area, the continent's third-largest country after Sudan and Algeria — which country?
Zaire: Country in Central Africa (1965–1997). With a population of over 23 million, Zaire was the most populous Francophone country in Africa.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Georges Dumézil (born 1898) is the earliest of the four. Dumézil is well known for his formulation of the trifunctional hypothesis on Proto-Indo-European mythology and society.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four began earliest?
Python (programming language) (founded 1991) is the earliest of the four. Python supports multiple programming paradigms but with an emphasis on object-oriented programming and dynamic typing.
Which of these four dates back furthest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Williamina Fleming is an astronomer. Williamina Paton Stevens Fleming (15 May 1857 – 21 May 1911) was a Scottish astronomer.
Who among these is a mathematician?
Carl Friedrich Gauss is a mathematician. Gauss was director of the Göttingen Observatory in Germany and professor of astronomy from 1807 until his death in 1855.
What is the atomic number of Rutherfordium?
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rf and atomic number 104.
What is the atomic number of Selenium?
Selenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Se and atomic number 34.
In what year was Buzz Aldrin born?
Buzz Aldrin ( AWL-drin; born Edwin Eugene Aldrin Jr.; January 20, 1930) is an American former astronaut, aeronautical engineer, and fighter pilot.
In what year was Christine Lagarde born?
Christine Lagarde: Lagarde had also served in the Government of France, most prominently as Minister of the Economy, Finance and Industry from 2007 until 2011.
In what year was Ernest Rutherford born?
Ernest Rutherford: Together with Thomas Royds, Rutherford is credited with proving that alpha radiation is composed of helium nuclei.
In what year did Arthur Conan Doyle die?
Arthur Conan Doyle: Sir Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle (22 May 1859 – 7 July 1930) was a British writer and physician.
In what year did Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz die?
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz: Leibniz, along with René Descartes and Baruch Spinoza, was one of the three influential early modern rationalists.
In what year was Oxygen discovered?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
Potassium chloride: Pfizer. Potassium chloride (KCl, or potassium salt) is a metal halide salt composed of potassium and chlorine.
Rendang: Indonesia. It refers to both a cooking method of frying and the dish cooked in that way.
Who is credited with discovering Musca?
Musca: Petrus Plancius. Musca (Latin for 'the fly') is a small constellation in the deep southern sky.
Who is credited with discovering Testosterone?
Testosterone: János Freud. Testosterone is the primary male sex hormone and androgen in males.
Who is credited with discovering Cyanoacrylate?
Cyanoacrylate: Harry Coover. The cyanoacrylate group in the monomer rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water to form long, strong chains.
Who is credited with discovering Rubidium?
Rubidium: Robert Bunsen. Rubidium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rb and atomic number 37.
This Swiss chemist discovered the structure of chitin in 1929 and decades later authored a memoir titled 'LSD: My Problem Child' — who was he?
Albert Hofmann (11 January 1906 - 29 April 2008) was a Swiss chemist known for being the first to synthesize, ingest, and learn of the psychedelic effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD).
Closely related to Hepatica and Pulsatilla, which flowering plant genus in the buttercup family is nicknamed the windflower?
Anemone is a genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.

In 2003, this American mountaineer amputated his own trapped forearm with a dull pocket knife after five days pinned by a boulder in a Utah canyon, then rappelled and hiked miles to safety — who is he?

Aron Ralston (born October 27, 1975) is an American mountaineer, mechanical engineer, and motivational speaker, known for surviving a canyoneering accident in 2003 by cutting off part of his own right arm.
This facial hair grows on the jaw, chin, and cheeks, most commonly in adult men, though some women develop it too in a condition called hirsutism — name it?
Beard is the hair that grows on the jaw, chin, upper lip, lower lip, cheeks, and neck of humans and some non-human animals.

This general medical term describes blood escaping a damaged vessel, whether internally or through a puncture in the skin, with the loss of more than about 15 percent of total volume proving potentially fatal. What is it called?
Bleeding is blood escaping from the circulatory system from damaged blood vessels.

Naturally green and yellow with scalloped black markings, this small, long-tailed seed-eating parrot native to Australia is bred worldwide in colors from blue to white — which bird, also called a budgie?
Budgerigar (--ree-; Melopsittacus undulatus), also known as the common parakeet, shell parakeet or budgie, is a small, long-tailed, seed-eating parrot native to Australia.

Which German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist discovered oxygen — though Priestley published first — and identified elements like molybdenum, tungsten, and chlorine before reportedly dying of mercury poisoning?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele (9 December 1742 - 21 May 1786) was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist.
A sweet-smelling, dense, colorless liquid with the formula CHCl3, this solvent doubled as an inhaled anesthetic from the 19th century into the early 20th. What is it?
Chloroform (often abbreviated as TCM), is an organochloride with the formula CHCl3 and a common solvent.

This icy small body from the outer Solar System develops a glowing atmosphere called a coma, and sometimes a tail, as it warms and releases gases when passing near the Sun — name this celestial object?
Comet is an icy, small Solar System body or interstellar object that warms and begins to release gases when passing close to the Sun, a process called outgassing.
This bird family, the sole one in its taxonomic order, includes roadrunners, koels, malkohas, and coucals across roughly 150 species. Name the family?
Cuckoo are birds in the family Cuculidae, the sole taxon in the order Cuculiformes.
Mother of Princess Alia, this royal later remarried a senior PLO official in 1970 after her short-lived marriage to Jordan's king ended — who is she?
Dina bint Abdul-Hamid (15 December 1929 - 21 August 2019) was a Hashemite princess and Queen of Jordan from 1955 until 1957 as the first wife of King Hussein.

This is the industrial process of converting other forms of energy into electric power, typically at power plants using electromechanical devices, before it is transmitted and distributed to end users. What is this process called?
Electricity generation is the process of generating electric power from sources of primary energy.

This genus of 700-plus flowering trees gets its name from Greek words meaning 'well covered' — a nod to the little cap fused over its stamens — and most species are native to Australia. The leafy 'gum trees' in question are which?
Eucalyptus is a genus of more than 700 species of flowering plants in the family Myrtaceae.
This infection and inflammation of hair follicles produces white-tipped pimples anywhere on hair-covered skin, and is considered a distinct condition from acne. Name it?
Folliculitis is the infection and inflammation of one or more hair follicles.
This branch of medicine has no set starting age, instead guided by a patient's needs and available caregiving, and helps those managing multiple chronic conditions — what is it?
Geriatrics is a medical specialty focused on addressing the unique health needs of older adults.
A French polymath dabbling in anthropology, medicine and physics, he's best remembered for an 1895 book that became a seminal work of crowd psychology — who was he?
Gustave Le Bon (7 May 1841 - 13 December 1931) was a leading French polymath whose areas of interest included anthropology, psychology, sociology, medicine, invention, and physics.
Serving as both Reichsbank president and Minister of Economics under Hitler, this economist was credited with Germany's 1930s 'economic miracle' even as he opposed aspects of rearmament — who is he?
Hjalmar Schacht (22 January 1877 - 3 June 1970) was a German economist, banker, politician, and co-founder of the German Democratic Party.
This medieval Arab scholar, considered a forerunner of modern sociology and economics, wrote his most famous work, an introduction to history known as the Muqaddimah, in just six months — who is he?
Ibn Khaldun (27 May 1332 - 17 March 1406, 732-808 AH) was an Arab scholar, historian, philosopher, and sociologist.

This American physicist worked on the Manhattan Project, then in 1949 proposed that — contrary to belief — not all atomic nuclei are spherical, an idea Aage Bohr later helped confirm. Who won a share of the 1975 Nobel for it?
James Rainwater (December 9, 1917 - May 31, 1986) was an American physicist who shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1975 for his part in determining the asymmetrical shapes of certain atomic nuclei.

The first woman of Indian origin to fly to space, this astronaut and aerospace engineer first studied in India before earning advanced degrees in the US and flying aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in 1997 — who was she?
Kalpana Chawla (July 1, 1962 - February 1, 2003) was an Indian-American astronaut and aerospace engineer who was the first woman of Indian origin to fly to space.

Seen using a silver stain and grown on media containing the amino acid cysteine, this genus of bacteria causes a severe pneumonia-like illness as well as a milder flu-like illness called Pontiac fever — name the genus?
Legionella is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria that can be seen using a silver stain or grown in a special media that contains cysteine, an amino acid.

Ranging across Eurasia with plumage of black, white, pink, and grey, this small insectivorous bird forms compact family flocks of six to seventeen outside the breeding season, its northern subspecies sporting all-white heads — which bird?
Long-tailed tit (Aegithalos caudatus) is a common bird species belonging to the bushtit family found throughout Eurasia.

Dubbed "sea locusts" by the ancient Assyrians and "prawn killers" elsewhere, these burrow-dwelling marine crustaceans are among the top predators of tropical shallows — yet they remain poorly understood. What are they?
Mantis shrimp are carnivorous marine crustaceans of the order Stomatopoda (from Ancient Greek (stma) 'mouth' and (pos) 'foot').

This chemical compound, typically administered by vein injection, is primarily used to treat methemoglobinemia and was used for over a century against malaria. Common side effects include headache, nausea, and vomiting. What is it?
Methylene blue is a salt used as a dye and as a medication.
This Bangladeshi economist pioneered microcredit and founded Grameen Bank, work that earned him the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize before he later led an interim government — who is he?
Muhammad Yunus (born 28 June 1940) is a Bangladeshi economist and statesman.

Discovered in a fossil-rich West African formation and first described in 1976 but not formally named until 1999, this rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur lived roughly 115 to 105 million years ago — which genus?
Nigersaurus is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur that lived during the middle Cretaceous period, about 115 to 105 million years ago.

Sitting in life's hierarchy between tissue and a full body system, this term describes a group of different tissues — like the epithelial and muscle layers of the gut wall — joined to serve one shared function. What is it?
Organ (biology) is a collection of tissues joined in a structural unit to serve a common function.
This pulse crop, given the scientific name Pisum sativum by Linnaeus in 1753, is usually eaten as a vegetable via its small round seeds. What is it?
Pea is a pulse or fodder crop, but the word often refers to the seed or sometimes the pod of this flowering plant species.
Odorless when pure but reeking of rotting fish in technical grade, this colorless PH3 gas can burst into a luminous flame on contact with air — what highly toxic compound is it?
Phosphine (IUPAC name: phosphane) is a colorless, flammable, highly toxic compound with the chemical formula PH3, classed as a pnictogen hydride.

Attacks of this condition — abdominal pain, vomiting, and confusion lasting days to weeks — stem from a buildup of porphyrins and can be triggered by stress, smoking, or certain medications. What is it?
Porphyria (or) is a group of disorders in which substances called porphyrins build up in the body, adversely affecting the skin or nervous system.
Found in nucleic acids as the building block behind adenine and guanine, this nitrogen-rich heterocyclic compound is the most common of its kind in nature — what is it?
Purine is a heterocyclic aromatic organic compound that consists of two rings (pyrimidine and imidazole) fused together.
Named from Greek words for 'rose' and 'tree,' this genus of over 1,000 woody flowering plant species serves as the national flower of Nepal and the state flower of Washington — what is it?

Rhododendron (pl.: rhododendra), from Ancient Greek (rhdon), meaning "rose", and (dndron), meaning "tree", is a very large genus of about 1,024 species of woody plants in the heath family (Ericaceae).
Arising from connective tissues like bone, cartilage, muscle, and fat, this rare cancer of mesenchymal cells makes up just 1% of adult diagnoses but 15% of childhood ones. What is it?
Sarcoma is a rare type of cancer that arises from cells of mesenchymal origin.
Named for its enormous shoe-shaped bill, this grey wading bird of East African swamps was once filed with storks but now sits beside pelicans — and its closest kin is the hamerkop — what is it?
Shoebill (Balaeniceps rex), also known as the whale-headed stork, whalebill, and shoe-billed stork, is a large long-legged wading bird.

Native to China and Vietnam, this invasive planthopper species has spread destructively across the US, feasting on grapevines and stone fruit as well as its preferred invasive host tree — what insect is it?
Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is a species of planthopper indigenous to parts of China and Vietnam.
This West African berry contains a molecule that binds so powerfully to taste buds that sour foods eaten afterward taste sweet instead — what's this plant's common nickname?
Synsepalum dulcificum is a plant in the Sapotaceae family, native to tropical Africa.

This weakly radioactive silvery metal, atomic number 90, tarnishes olive-grey in air, and its most stable isotope has a half-life of about 14 billion years — roughly the age of the universe. What element is this?
Thorium is a chemical element; it has symbol Th and atomic number 90.

It spawned a maritime patrol version (the Tu-142) and even a passenger airliner (the Tu-114), and Russia expects to keep flying this propeller-driven bomber until at least 2040 — which aircraft is it?
Tupolev Tu-95 (NATO reporting name: "Bear") is a Soviet nuclear-capable large, four-engine turboprop strategic bomber and missile platform.

Belonging to the same family as kangaroos, this informally named group of smaller macropods is native to Australia and New Guinea, with introduced populations as far away as Hawaii and the UK — what are they called?
Wallaby is a small or middle-sized macropod native to Australia and New Guinea, with introduced populations in New Zealand, Hawaii, the United Kingdom and other countries.
Also called humped cattle for the fatty growth on its shoulders, this South Asian breed group is used for everything from plowing to dairy, and even kept as pets in miniature form — what is it?
Zebu (Bos indicus), also known as indicine cattle and humped cattle, is a species or subspecies of domestic cattle originating in South Asia.

Typically affecting women between 35 and 50, this uterine condition occurs when endometrial-like tissue grows within the muscular wall of the uterus, causing painful, heavy periods — what is it called?
Adenomyosis: Extension of endometrial tissue into the myometrium.
On 18 March 1965, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first person to walk in space, spending over twelve minutes outside his capsule during a Voskhod mission — who is he?

Capable of constantly changing its shape by extending and retracting temporary 'false feet,' this single-celled organism turns up across nearly every branch of the eukaryotic tree of life — what is it?

Their larvae — nicknamed "doodlebugs" in North America for the marks they leave — dig sandy pits to trap passing ants, while the dusk-flying adults are often mistaken for dragonflies. What insect is this?
His namesake effect — scattered X-rays losing energy — proved light behaves as particles and earned a share of the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics. Who was this American physicist?
Discovered by Robert Koch in 1876, this rod-shaped microbe was the first ever shown experimentally to cause disease, providing the earliest evidence for germ theory — which organism?
Strawberries, blueberries, blackberries, and currants all fall under this small, pulpy, often brightly colored category of fruit — which Britain calls "soft fruit." What is it?
Berry: In the culinary sense, small edible fruit.
Launched in 1993 as a redesigned-wing, glass-cockpit upgrade of an earlier narrow-body jetliner series, this aircraft competes chiefly against the Airbus A320 family — which aircraft is it?
Boeing 737 Next Generation: Single-aisle airliner family.
This volatile red-brown liquid element, with properties between chlorine and iodine, gets its name from the Greek word for 'stench' — which element?
Bromine: Chemical element with atomic number 35 (Br)
Designated Maryland's official state crustacean, this species is expected to benefit from climate change even as overfishing hurts other Chesapeake Bay fisheries — which species?
Callinectes sapidus: Species of crustacean. It is Maryland's largest commercial fishery and has been designated its state crustacean.
A wartime myth claimed eating this vegetable helped British pilots see in the dark — really a cover story for radar — which root vegetable?
Carrot: Root vegetable. The carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus) is a root vegetable in the umbellifer family Apiaceae.
Holder of 186 patents, this American engineer ran research at General Motors for nearly three decades and gave the world the electric car starter, leaded gasoline, and Freon — who was he?
Charles F. Kettering: American inventor, engineer and businessman (1876–1958)
Despite its common 'cat' nickname, this small nocturnal mammal from Africa and Asia is not a feline at all — and one African species yields a musky scent long used in perfumery — what is it?
Civet: Mammals of the families Viverridae and Nandiniidae and the genus Fossa.

A member of the true thrushes, this Eurasian songbird whose nominate male is all black breeds across Europe, western Asia, and North Africa and has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand — which bird is it?
Common blackbird: Thrush native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa.
Smelling of vanilla but tasting bitter, which plant compound isn't itself an anticoagulant, though its derivatives inspired the blood-thinning drug warfarin?
This Zambian-born economist turned heads with four New York Times bestsellers, including "Dead Aid," which argues that foreign aid actually holds Africa back. Which author and life peer is it?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo: Zambian-born economist (born February 1969)
Known for feigning death when cornered, which genus of cat-sized marsupials includes the only marsupial species found north of Mexico?
Didelphis: Genus of marsupials. The six species in the genus Didelphis, commonly known as Large American opossums, are members of the opossum order, Didelphimorphia.
Nicknamed 'Viking disease,' this hand condition — first surgically treated in 1831 by the surgeon it's named after — permanently curls the ring finger inward. What is it?
Dupuytren's contracture: Medical condition featuring permanent bending of fingers.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
Sold under the brand name Pepcid, this H2-receptor-blocking medication treats stomach-acid conditions like peptic ulcers and begins working within an hour — which drug?
Famotidine: Medication that reduces stomach acid.
Also nicknamed 'muscae volitantes' — Latin for flying flies — these tiny shadowy specks drift across your vision, especially noticeable against a blank blue sky. What are they?
Floater: Deposits within the eye's vitreous humour.

Nicknamed for their nighttime cries, these small nocturnal African primates are, according to the African Wildlife Foundation, the continent's most successful strepsirrhine group — what are they commonly called?
Galago: Family of primates. The Ghanaian name aposor is given to them because of their firm grip on branches.
Caused by a genetic variant in the UGT1A1 gene, this harmless liver condition slows the breakdown of bilirubin and can trigger jaundice during stress, exercise, or fasting — what is it called?
Gilbert's syndrome: Medical condition. It is typically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and occasionally in an autosomal dominant pattern depending on the type of variant.
An Augustinian friar and abbot in Brno, this Austrian biologist spent 1856 to 1863 crossbreeding pea plants — work that earned him posthumous fame as the founder of genetics. Who was he?
Gregor Mendel: Austrian biologist and friar (1822–1884)

This English physician co-wrote the first English-language medical textbook on homosexuality in 1897, coined the term 'narcissism,' and penned an early public account of a mescaline trip he took on himself. Who was he?
Havelock Ellis: British physician, eugenicist, writer, and social reformer (1859–1939)
Its name means 'river horse' in Ancient Greek, yet this semiaquatic sub-Saharan giant — the largest even-toed ungulate alive — is more closely tied to pigs than to horses; what is it?
Hippopotamus: Species of large semi-aquatic mammal.
This huge insect order includes sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants, and its females often carry an egg-laying tube that doubles as a stinger — what order is it?
Hymenoptera: Order of insects. Over 150,000 living species of Hymenoptera have been described, in addition to over 2,000 extinct ones.
Fever, sore throat, body aches and fatigue that start one to four days after exposure and may spiral into pneumonia — there are four types of this viral infection. What is it?

Alongside Francis Crick, which American biologist co-proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in a 1953 Nature paper, building on the work of Rosalind Franklin, earning a share of the 1962 Nobel Prize?
This French mathematician ranged across number theory, complex analysis, and mathematical physics — and a crater on the Moon is named after him; who was he?
Often miscalled a 'bear,' this tailless, fluffy-eared Australian marsupial is actually a close cousin of the wombat — what is it?
Koala: Arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to Australia.
Called a 'universal genius,' this Swiss polymath founded graph theory and topology while introducing much of modern mathematical notation — who is he?
The third wide-body airliner to enter service after the 747 and DC-10, this trijet used an S-duct to route its third engine through the tail — which aircraft?

Lockheed L-1011 TriStar: American wide-body trijet airliner. The Lockheed L-1011 TriStar (pronounced "El-ten-eleven") is an American medium-to-long-range, wide-body trijet airliner built by the Lockheed Corporation.
A chemical engineer and physician who also served in the Peace Corps, she became the first African-American woman in space aboard Endeavour in 1992 — who is she?
Mae Jemison: American astronaut, doctor and engineer (born 1956)

This field studies abstract things like numbers, shapes, sets and probabilities, using logical proof to establish truths it calls theorems — and its branches include algebra, geometry and number theory. What is it?
Mathematics: Field of knowledge. Mathematics is a field of knowledge concerned with abstract concepts such as numbers, geometric shapes, sets, functions, and probabilities.
Sold under the brand Glucophage, this first-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes is favored partly because it isn't associated with weight gain. What drug is it?
Metformin: Medication used to treat diabetes.
Sold as Remeron, this atypical tetracyclic antidepressant is often chosen when depression comes tangled with anxiety or insomnia — which drug is it?
Mirtazapine: Antidepressant medication. Mirtazapine, sold under the brand name Remeron among others, is an atypical tetracyclic antidepressant, and as such is used primarily to treat depression.

Made of contractile proteins called actin and myosin, this soft tissue exists in three vertebrate forms — skeletal, cardiac, and smooth — and forms during a developmental process called myogenesis — what is it?
Muscle: Important Biological tissue that allows movement.
Named after a German physical chemist, this electrochemistry formula calculates a reaction's reduction potential from temperature, electron count, and reactant concentrations — which relationship?
Nernst equation: Physical law in electrochemistry.
Represented by symbols like '11' in the Hindu-Arabic system used worldwide, these mathematical objects serve to count, measure, and label — what are they called?
Number: Used to count, measure, and label. The most basic examples are the natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so forth.
Nicknamed 'brittle bone disease,' this genetic disorder causes fragile bones and blue-tinted eye whites, usually stemming from faulty type I collagen — what is it?
Osteogenesis imperfecta: Group of genetic disorders resulting in fragile bones.

Also called the blue passionflower, this South American vine climbs via tendrils to 10 metres, bears fragrant blue-white blooms with a fringed coronal filament, and produces an edible but not particularly tasty orange fruit — which plant is it?
Passiflora caerulea: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.
Synthesized in 1938 by German chemist Otto Eisleb and later marketed as Demerol, this synthetic opioid was the go-to pain medication for much of the 20th century — what is it?
Pethidine: Opioid analgesic. Pethidine, also known as meperidine and sold under the brand name Demerol among others, is a fully synthetic opioid pain medication of the phenylpiperidine class.
